author: Progressive International
title: When the Bargain Breaks
content:
On 23 September, Spanish police evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for 71 years. After buying her flat, property company Urbagestión had sought to increase Abascal’s rent to more than her monthly pension. Neighbours had prevented three previous attempts to evict her. The fourth succeeded. Abascal was carried out of her home on a stretcher and taken to hospital. The eviction was lawful.

Tens of thousands marched through Madrid in outrage. Protesters occupied Puerta del Sol, erecting more than 1,200 tents, complete with named streets and a makeshift medical centre. They demanded rent controls, protection against eviction and an end to housing speculation. Parliament rejected two emergency housing decrees, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election for 29 November. On 7 October, Abascal died in hospital, one day before she was due to sign an agreement allowing her to return home.

Across the Pyrenees, a protest that began at a secondary school in a Paris suburb has become a national uprising. Lycée Saint-Exupéry was missing 13 teachers, a deputy head and essential support staff. Students and teachers walked out. Within days, blockades and other disruptions had spread to more than 1,000 schools. title: Meta Discovers New Tool to Sabotage Lula’s Campaign
content:
It is no secret that Lula’s campaign is facing a David versus Goliath battle. As many people have put it, this is “the toughest and most decisive campaign of our lives.” When we look at how much big tech is investing in efforts to boost Brazil’s far right, we begin to understand just how much is at stake in this election. The direction Brazil takes over the next few years will have profound consequences for a world increasingly dominated by groups that hold the machinery to grind ordinary people into the dirt.

Last week, I wrote that a confidential source working at Meta Brazil had told me that the company, controlled by Donald Trump’s close friend Mark Zuckerberg, had carried out mass layoffs of its content moderators. It replaced a significant portion of its staff with machines and artificial intelligence systems that now decide what can and cannot be published in Brazil. The change came precisely during the election campaign. No, your algorithm did not suddenly go haywire by sheer coincidence. There are external commands and interventions at work.

Now another cobra strike by the all powerful tech giant has come to light: sabotage through WhatsApp.

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: From Haile Selassie to Abiy Ahmed: the Human Cost of Imperial Nostalgia
content:
The irony is difficult to escape. Haile Selassie became a symbol of resistance to foreign aggression while denying Eritreans the right to self-determination. Abiy Ahmed was rewarded for accepting Eritrea’s internationally recognized border, yet within a few years his government began advancing claims to sovereign access to the Red Sea. The very territorial settlement that helped earn him the Nobel Peace Prize now stands in tension with his maritime ambitions.

Both men benefited enormously from international recognition. Their reputations gave them prestige and influence, but those reputations have too often overshadowed the suffering of the people under their rule. Haile Selassie’s imperial government suppressed resistance in Tigray and annexed Eritrea. Under Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopia has endured devastating wars, while his government’s Red Sea rhetoric has renewed Eritrean fears of territorial aggression.

I have written about the dangers of romanticizing Ethiopia’s imperial past, most recently in Imperial Nostalgia: History, Sovereignty, and the Unfinished Work of Decolonization in the Horn of Africa. What concerns me today is that this nostalgia is no longer confined to history books or monuments. It has returned to contemporary politics, and the consequences could be catastrophic for another generation of Ethiopians and Eritreans.

Haile Selassie’s reputation rests heavily on his resistance to Italian fascism. His appearance before the League of Nations in 1936 became one of the defining moments of his international career. But the familiar account gives the emperor far more prominence than the people who actually fought the occupation.

Haile Selassie left Ethiopia in 1936 and spent the following years in Britain. Meanwhile, Ethiopian patriots remained behind, fighting a brutal occupation. They lived in the mountains, organized resistance, endured enormous hardship and risked their lives. The emperor became the international face of their struggle, but he was not the one carrying its daily burden.

Consider Belay Zeleke, one of the patriots who fought the Italians. After the emperor returned to power, Belay came into conflict with the imperial government. In January 1945, he was executed alongside his brother and other associates. Think about the irony. A man who had fought foreign occupation was hanged under the authority of an emperor celebrated around the world for resisting that same occupation.

The emperor’s record in Tigray reveals another contradiction. In 1943, when people in Tigray rose against imperial authority during the first Woyane uprising, Haile Selassie turned to Britain for military assistance. British Royal Air Force aircraft bombed Mekelle and other locations. As Human Rights Watch documented, British air power helped suppress resistance to the imperial government.

Here was an emperor celebrated for standing against European aggression using European aircraft against people resisting his own rule. How does that fit the image of a champion of freedom?

Haile Selassie’s reputation as a Pan-Africanist also deserves scrutiny. His role in establishing the Organization of African Unity in Addis Ababa in 1963 was important. But diplomatic achievement should not be confused with a consistent commitment to African freedom.

Haile Selassie and his foreign minister, Ketema Yifru, worked to establish Ethiopia as a center of African diplomacy. Hosting the OAU gave the emperor enormous prestige. Yet the same government was denying Eritreans the right to determine their future.

Eritrea’s federal autonomy had been systematically dismantled before Haile Selassie annexed the territory in 1962. While the emperor was celebrated as a defender of African independence, Eritreans were beginning a liberation struggle that would last thirty years.

The OAU largely treated Eritrea as an internal Ethiopian matter. Its silence is especially striking when compared with Western Sahara. The organization admitted the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic despite Morocco’s fierce opposition. It was prepared to confront one African government over self-determination but failed to extend comparable recognition to Eritreans struggling against Ethiopian rule.

The romanticization of Haile Selassie reached extraordinary heights through the Rastafari movement. Emerging from racial oppression in Jamaica, the movement invested in the Ethiopian emperor with immense spiritual and political significance. For some Rastafarians, he became a divine figure.

I understand the longing for African dignity that helped produce this reverence. But the status bestowed on Haile Selassie was profoundly misplaced. The emperor imagined as a symbol of Black liberation presided over an authoritarian state that denied freedom to many of the people under its control.

There is another irony. The Shah of Iran and Mobutu Sese Seko are widely remembered for their repression. Haile Selassie has been treated differently. In 2019, the African Union unveiled a statue in his honor at its Addis Ababa headquarters.

What does such a monument tell Eritreans whose independence he denied? What does it tell Tigrayans whose communities were bombed under his government, or the families of patriots executed after fighting Italian occupation?

In 1972, Haile Selassie celebrated his eightieth birthday with imperial extravagance. Hunger and deprivation were already part of life in the countryside, and the famine that devastated Wollo and Tigray in the following years exposed the extraordinary distance between the imperial court and the people it governed.

The images of starving Ethiopians became inseparable from those of imperial luxury. They revealed a political order in which the grandeur of the ruler could coexist with the desperation of his subjects.

More than half a century later, Tigrayans have again endured hunger, displacement and the destruction of their livelihoods. The war that began in 2020 devastated agriculture, markets, health services and entire communities. The Pretoria Agreement was supposed to bring peace and recovery, yet its implementation remained deeply contested, and renewed fighting has placed civilians under further pressure.

At the same time, Abiy Ahmed has pursued monumental construction projects, including the enormous Chaka palace development. Reporting on the project has described its extraordinary scale.

Abiy presents these projects as evidence of national renewal. But what kind of renewal is meaningful to a family struggling to find food? What does the magnificence of a palace mean to people who have lost their homes, farms and children to war?

The comparison is not simply between Haile Selassie’s birthday celebration and Abiy’s construction projects. It concerns the priorities of rulers who seek grandeur while ordinary people struggle to survive.

Ethiopia’s successive conflicts have consumed the lives of young people, many from impoverished rural communities. Reports of coercive recruitment raise grave questions about how the state obtains manpower for its wars. Critics have described mass infantry assaults as human wave tactics, exposing large numbers of soldiers to devastating casualties.

These young people are not abstractions. They have parents, brothers, sisters and children. Many have little influence over the decisions that send them to the battlefield. Rulers speak of greatness and destiny. Poor families bury their children.

In important respects, Haile Selassie and Abiy Ahmed have fought variations of the same wars. Both periods have been marked by violent struggles over centralized authority and the political rights of peoples within Ethiopia. Both have involved devastating military campaigns in Tigray. And both bring us back to Ethiopian ambitions toward Eritrea.

The historical circumstances are different. Haile Selassie denied Eritreans self-determination. Abiy governs a country that must recognize Eritrea as an independent state. But the political temptation is familiar: presenting the ambitions of rulers as the necessities of the nation.

Eritrea paid an extraordinary price for independence. While many African countries achieved independence through negotiated transfers of power, Eritreans endured thirty years of armed struggle from 1961 to 1991. Algeria, Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau, Zimbabwe and Namibia also experienced prolonged liberation wars, but Eritrea’s experience was especially bitter because much of independent Africa failed to recognize its claim.

Generations of Eritrea’s finest young people sacrificed their education, professions, families and lives. Some never had the opportunity to build the futures they imagined. Others survived only to carry the memories of those who did not.

Their sacrifice is the foundation of Eritrea’s sovereignty.

Ethiopia’s inland geography creates economic challenges, but it does not confer a right to annex Eritrean ports or coastline. Commercial access can be negotiated between sovereign countries. Territorial sovereignty is an entirely different matter.

The language of sea access must not obscure that distinction. Eritreans hear echoes of the imperial claims against which their parents and grandparents fought.

For nearly three years, since Abiy began publicly advancing Ethiopia’s demand for sovereign access to the Red Sea in 2023, Ethiopian officials have repeatedly invoked geography, population, history and economic necessity. What is presented internationally as a question of access has increasingly raised the prospect of territorial control.

This is the deeper threat that international diplomacy must confront, rather than treating the present crisis as though it appeared overnight.

On October 5, the European Union warned of escalating violence and called for restraint and respect for sovereignty. On October 14, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Abiy Ahmed about de-escalation, territorial integrity and avoiding cross-border incursions.

These principles are necessary. But appeals directed equally at both countries risk obscuring the political origins of the confrontation. There is a difference between advancing a claim to another country’s coastline and defending an internationally recognized border. Diplomacy should not erase that distinction.

The contradiction became especially apparent when Ethiopia accused Eritrea of an invasion in a letter to the United Nations Security Council. Eritrea rejected the accusation and, arguing that Ethiopia’s campaign for sovereign access to the Red Sea had created the danger.

The competing allegations about military movements deserve independent examination. But Ethiopia’s diplomatic accusation should not make the preceding three years disappear. International attention can quickly shift to the latest claim of victimhood while overlooking the rhetoric that helped produce the confrontation.

This is how political framing reshapes the public understanding of a conflict. A government advancing territorial ambitions presents itself as the threatened party, and the historical origins of the dispute are pushed aside.

The African Union has its own responsibility. It honors Haile Selassie while failing to confront the historical denial of Eritrean self-determination. Its mediation of the Pretoria Agreement has also been followed by renewed fighting and continuing humanitarian suffering. The United States and Europe cannot limit their response to warnings while overlooking the territorial ambitions that have contributed to the crisis.

Nor should criticism of Ethiopian rulers excuse the conduct of Eritrea’s government. Eritreans paid a terrible price during the 2020 to 2022 war. Defending Eritrean sovereignty does not require defending Isaias Afwerki’s decisions or accepting the sacrifice of Eritrean lives in wars that need not have been fought.

Haile Selassie’s Pan-African credentials could not justify the denial of Eritrean independence. Abiy Ahmed’s Nobel Peace Prize, palaces and promises of national greatness cannot justify another generation of suffering.

History repeats itself when old claims of domination return in new language, when human suffering becomes the price of national greatness, and when international institutions fail to distinguish the rights of peoples from the ambitions of rulers.

Africa does not need another emperor, another seventh king or another generation sacrificed to imperial nostalgia. It needs governments that respect their peoples and the sovereignty of their neighbors.

The measure of a leader should not be the size of his palace, the grandeur of his monument or the wars fought in his name. It should be whether ordinary people can live in peace, feed their families and build futures without being asked to die for someone else’s ambitions.

author: Phil Wilson
title: Wisconsin Gubernatorial Candidate, Carlos LeMar Dixon, Joins the Class Struggle in Northampton, Massachusetts
content:
Northampton, Massachusetts masquerades as one of the most progressive cities in America – a place where police raided a homeless encampment and took away warm clothes on a cold, rainy “Columbus Day” weekend two years ago. In Northampton we manufacture armaments to reduce Gaza to rubble. We underfund our schools, attempt to build gaudy renewal projects to attract gentrification, but the city council convenes beneath an austere portrait of Frederick Douglas. We are a cauldron of pretense, indifference, hope and confusion – as American as apple pie. My wife, Shelly, and I have lived here among wonderful neighbors and friends for more than three decades, but like everywhere else we are cleaved into irreconcilable segments – rich and poor, working class and managerial class, college professors and tent city residents.

At 11PM on a Wednesday night I am walking fast down Prospect Street in Northampton, Massachusetts with our house guest, Carlos LeMar Dixon – a write-in candidate for Governor of Wisconsin. It’s a long story. Our pace might be brisk, but our discussion floats leisurely, expansively encompassing an array of topics from war and ecology to NBA basketball. We undoubtedly get a few double-takes from the occasional late night driver passing by – me: old, weathered and white, Carlos: long, lean and Black, almost a foot taller and young enough to be unnoticed if he stepped off

author: Tings Chak
title: How Brazil’s Election Could Reshape Relations with China
content:
On 25 October, Brazilians will return to the polls to choose between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in an attempted coup. The first round gave Flávio 47.03 per cent of valid votes against Lula’s 45.16 per cent, revealing the enduring strength of the far right four years after its electoral defeat. The runoff takes place as Donald Trump seeks to restore US domination over Latin America, with Brazil emerging as a consequential battleground in Washington’s campaign to contain China’s growing relations with the region.

Over the past two decades, Brazil and China have built a political partnership that has expanded the space for independent action among countries of the Global South. Under Lula and Xi Jinping, this relationship has deepened through cooperation in industrial development, infrastructure, science, and technology. The election will determine whether this project advances or Brazil’s international orientation is subordinated to Washington’s renewed Monroe Doctrine as part of the continent’s rightward shift.

Since Lula’s return to the presidency in 2023, the two governments have connected Chinese cooperation with Brazil’s development programmes, including Nova Indústria Brasil, the Growth Acceleration Programme (PAC), and the Ecological Transformation

author: Michael Albert
title: Liberating Theory: Vision and Strategy
content:
[This article ends the sequence from the seven author book Liberating Theory—by myself, Leslie Cagan, Noam Chomsky, Robin Hahnel, Mel King, Lydia Sargent, and Holly Sklar—published in 1986. This time the collective discussed vision and strategy. We here excerpt two chapters and their dialogues.]

So far, four sources of definition for society, not one or even two. A human center and institutional boundary, not an economic base and social superstructure. Accommodation, co-definition, and even co-reproduction between components all within an encompassing ecology and international relations. Social stability and/or social transformation. Three potential ruling classes, not two. Is all that and more just academic complex-ification or does it have simplifying implications for actual, worthy, workable vision and strategy?

Definitive evidence about the worth of these new concepts can only come from applying them to three critical questions: What features and dynamics characterize our society now? What is our vision of a more desirable future society? How do we expect to get from “here” to “there”?

Much has been written about the first question. While we hope that our holist principles will inform further analyses of contemporary conditions, we now focus our attention on the latter two questions.

Having argued so strenuously that societies are rarely if ever predominately determined

author: Bart Hawkins Kreps
title: Infrastructure, Finance, and the Sale of the Future
content:
Imagine yourself as a housing developer – an entrepreneur, a big-time player, a real deal-maker. Your people devise a plan to borrow money, buy land, design and win approval for a new subdivision, and sell 1,000 new housing units. Then, perhaps years before the houses are completed and decades before the initial mortgages are repaid, you sell your shares in the venture for a tidy profit. A neat trick, this, cashing in today on bills that others will pay long into the future.

You have become wealthier, but have you been a “wealth creator”? For that matter, are you contributing to “economic growth”? Where does the money come from for this venture: is it capital accumulated from the past, or is this money newly created the moment credit is extended by banks and off-setting debts are recorded on balance sheets?

These are among the many questions addressed by Timothy Mitchell in his new book The Alibi of Capital, out on March 10 from Verso.

Mitchell works his way through a profound rewriting of economic history and economic theory. He wants us to think carefully about who pays for what is labelled “economic growth.” Is the earning of interest some natural property of money? Why was the phrase “the economy” almost never used until the mid-20th century, while today the economy is routinely invoked as the determinant of what is politically, socially, or environmentally acceptable? author: Brasil 247
title: Celso Amorim Warns of U.S. Interference in Second Round Elections
content:
Ambassador Celso Amorim, special adviser to the presidency on international affairs, warned of the risk that the United States could interfere in Brazil’s election process. He said the October 25 presidential runoff carries consequences that reach far beyond Brazil’s borders. In an interview with Tutaméia on Friday, the former foreign and defense minister discussed pressure from the Trump administration on Latin America, the challenges facing Brazilian sovereignty, and the importance of the country’s technological and military independence.

Amorim said Brazil holds a strategic position in the global balance of power, and that the country’s political decisions have ripple effects across the Global South and relations between major powers.

“What happens in Brazil will have an influence on the global balance itself,” he said.

The diplomat stressed that Brazilian sovereignty depends on maintaining diverse international relationships and avoiding dependence on any single power.

“In the complex world we live in today, sovereignty doesn’t mean isolation. It means having relationships with more than one country. It means diversifying your relationships. It means not depending on a single power in any sense, economically, socioculturally, or even militarily in terms of defense,” he said.

author: Miguel Enrique Stédile
title: How Trump Tries to Decide the Elections in Brazil
content:
On the last Friday before the first round of Brazil’s presidential elections, the U.S. embassy and consulates in the country remained closed, following a generic order from the State Department regarding ‘security concerns.’ Elections in Brazil proceed peacefully; there are no civil conflicts or military threats, no records of political violence above normal levels, nor any threats to American citizens or diplomatic structures. But the decision, followed solely and inexplicably by the Australian embassy, is part of a set of actions by Washington to attempt to interfere in the Brazilian elections.

The actions began more than a year ago, when the United States linked increased tariffs on items imported from Brazil to the ongoing process to try former President Jair Bolsonaro for an attempted coup d’état. The relationship between political pressure to prevent the conviction of an ally and economic measures was publicized by the White House itself, as well as used to persecute the Supreme Court Justice responsible for the trial, blocking financial movements in the U.S. and preventing his entry into the country, and with ministers of the Lula da Silva government. author: Thomas Klikauer
title: German Car Workers Rally Against Job Cuts
content:
In September, 175,000 workers at 280 locations in Germany’s automotive and supplier industry engaged in a day of protest against the planned job cuts in the car industry. It shows that Germany’s workforce is prepared to fight for its jobs and its future. However, at several large Volkswagen (VW) locations, the true collective power of workers remained largely hidden behind factory gates.

At Volkswagen’s prime location in Wolfsburg, thousands gathered inside the factory gates. At an adjacent “public” rally only around 300 workers came. At Volkswagen’s Kassel-Baunatal location, about 850 workers took part in an “inside the factory” event, according to IGM’s Vertrauensleute, or union stewards. Representing workers in Germany’s still mighty car industry, the IGM union had planned for mostly union representatives [Vertrauensleute] to participate.

On the positive side, this might have been because IGM was unsure whether workers would follow its call to protest. On the downside, it might have been because the union wanted to confine the protest to its “controllable” union body rather than risk a true – and perhaps uncontrollable – protest by disgruntled workers against VW’s management. IGM wants to negotiate with that management and, as in the case of VW, has a relationship with it that is commonly seen as that of an assistant to management.

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: From Tigray to the Red Sea: Ethiopia’s War in a Wider Regional Struggle
content:
I am not a military expert, but I do not read the withdrawal of Tigrayan forces from towns as straightforward evidence that their military position has weakened. An army can leave towns, roads and airports without losing its ability to move, reorganize, coordinate and strike. The more important questions are whether the force remains intact, how mobile it is, whether it can coordinate across different fronts, and whether it can still choose where and when to engage.

That is how I look at what is happening around Mekelle. Reuters reported on October 2 that federal and allied forces were moving toward the Tigrayan capital, and the following day reported that they had retaken Alula Aba Nega Airport. On a conventional military map that looks like a major federal success. But the map may be giving us a false sense of what is actually happening.

Debretsion Gebremichael who is the president of Tigray had already announced a counteroffensive and said Tigrayan forces would not fight according to the government’s dictates. I therefore do not see their movement out of Mekelle as a setback. I see an orderly and deliberate withdrawal from a fixed urban position by a force whose leadership had already told us that it intended to choose a different battlefield.

author: Sonali Kolhatkar
title: An Abolitionist Vision for the World We Want
content:
A recent New York Times editorial by Tim Wu, a former antitrust adviser for the Biden administration, caught my eye for the criticism it leveled at Democrats for making affordability a central issue ahead of the midterm elections. Wu contends that the party needs to go further and focus not merely on the high price tags of necessities, but on the unfairness of the entire economic system.

While this is a refreshing shift in the right direction, it doesn’t go nearly far enough. It’s true that a majority of Americans across the political spectrum believe our economy is rigged in favor of the rich. But merely pointing out the obvious is unlikely to attract a huge shift in voting toward the Democratic Party.

Moreover, Wu says nothing about the racist rage that has defined President Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s decimation of our democracy, about the devastation to communities of color, immigrants, women, LGBTQ+ people, and other marginalized members of our society. Nor does he acknowledge the corporate harms that Democrats failed to tackle when they were in power and are now being accelerated under Republicans: fossil fuel emissions, tech domination, and AI, harms that disproportionately impactpoor people and people of color.

To Wu and most Democratic Party consultants, these issues are distinct and, depending on the cultural tides, are either worth tackling or anathema

author: Belen Fernandez
title: Corporate Media Don’t Understand the Houthis—and Don’t Want You to, Either
content:
It’s that time of year again: The Houthis are making the news—and so is the Western corporate media narrative that surrounds them.

The Houthis—formally Ansar Allah, “Supporters of God”—are from the Zaydi Shia minority in Yemen, and have governed the most populous sections of the country, including the capital Sanaa, since the start of Yemen’s civil war in 2014.

Like many a “civil” war, the conflict has plenty of outside participants—most notably Saudi Arabia, which led a coalition of Arab states (with the backing of the United States) in an effort to bomb and starve Yemen away from Houthi control.

In 2022, a tenuous truce took hold between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, but the Saudi blockade of the country was never lifted.

This July, the Houthis declared their own naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, in response to the Saudi siege and resumed bombing of Yemen. In a rapid September offensive, the group completed its takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea Coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait, putting Saudi oil shipping operations in a decisive bind. The Houthis have also launched missiles at Saudi Arabia in response to Saudi attacks on the country.

author: Yanis Varoufakis
title: The Centre-Left’s Slow Suicide
content:
“Only dangerous fanatics refuse to compromise,” my mother used to tell me. And so, several decades later, I entered government ready to compromise; a small price to pay, I thought, for delivering a modicum of relief to the suffering majority who had voted us in. Yet the hardest, and the most pertinent, question kept torturing me: how does one compromise without ending up compromised? Which single compromise would catapult me into the land of the co-opted? For months, I struggled to find the answer, until one revealed itself unexpectedly.

It is an enigma that begets a paradox. On the one hand, trying to pinpoint the pivotal compromise is as futile as trying to seek the single hair that, once lost, admits one into the brotherhood of the bald. On the other hand, just as one glance at me confirms I lack enough hair to count as bald, one glance at Andy Burnham and the vast majority of Europe’s centre-left leaders confirms they are compromised. It is a question that remains pertinent.

But at what point does compromise turn into defection? At what point does practicing the art of conceding judiciously lead one to betray one’s constituency — even to embrace villainy? Indeed, do the villains even know they are villains? Were they aware of a moment when their cascade of compromises finally pushed them beyond the moral pale? I doubt it. author: Ashir Naveed
title: The Power of a Label: How the Word “Terrorist” Kills
content:
“If these words reach you, know that Israel has succeeded in killing me and silencing my voice…Do not forget Gaza…And do not forget me in your sincere prayers for forgiveness and acceptance.”

These were the final words of Anas al-Sharif, written 4 months before he was killed by the Israeli military.

To the outside world, Anas was a journalist for Al Jazeera, reporting on the devastating siege of Gaza. But behind the camera, he was much more than that. The 28-year-old was a father of two young children. He was a husband. A son.

To the Israeli military, he was a terrorist.

Through his camera, the world watched fathers as they desperately dug through the rubble, searching for their missing children. They watched as he filmed doctors performing surgeries without electricity and proper tools. The world watched as he filmed young children, no more than skin and bones, waiting in lines to get food. Anas could have left anytime, saving himself and his family. But he didn’t. Despite multiple warnings from the Israeli military threatening to kill the young journalist, he stayed. Eventually, Anas became one of the last journalists in northern Gaza. His camera continued to show the devastation around him, as he became one of the last windows into Gaza.

author: C.J. Polychroniou
title: Trial of “ulm5” Activists is Further Evidence That Germany Increasingly Resembles a Police State
content:
Germany is a country with a long and complex relationship to authoritarianism. It is also of course the country that gave birth to the most evil political regime (Nazism) in the modern era.

The Allies agreed on the denazification of Germany as a goal after the end of World War II, but the general consensus is that it wasn’t a success. Some high-ranking Nazis were put on trial and sentenced to death, others were removed from public positions, but the majority of Nazis were reintegrated into postwar German society and even landed high-ranking positions.

Now, Germany is again displaying worrying signs of authoritarianism, as evidenced by the meteoric rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. However, Germany’s love affair with authoritarian rule runs deeper than the current surge of the AfD. Its legal and judicial system has become notorious for its restrictions on freedom of speech and its penchant for framing dissent “not as a democratic expression but as a threat to public order.”

The Ulm5 trial underway in Stuttgart, and now approaching its final stage, has exposed for all to see not only Germany’s increasingly neofascist playbook for silencing dissent but complicity in Israel’s genocide.

author: Gary Olson
title: Zionism Uber Alles
content:
Volkswagen (VW) began as the “people’s car” under Hitler but before long it was primarily producing military vehicles, V1 bombs and missiles for the Wehrmacht in World War II. Some 80 percent of the VW workers were forced labor, including prisoners from concentration camps, many of whom did not survive. The complex contained four concentration camps and eight forced-labor camps. In 1944, a VW engineer traveled to Auschwitz and selected 300 hundred skilled workers, (United States Holocaust Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia Volkswagen Facts). I’m hardly the first to note the grotesque irony that a company created by Hitler is reinventing itself on the same business model, this time to be complicit in another genocide.

The Osnabruck facility will be repurposed to manufacture military vehicles, heavy launchers and power generators for Israel’s Iron Dome. Unable to compete with Chinese electronic vehicles — profits fell 53 percent in 2015 — Volkswagen is shedding 100,000 jobs in the next few years and this conversion will guarantee that 1,200 positions will be preserved. Mercedes Benz, Audi, Daimler and BMW are all attempting to tap into ramped up defense spending to offset losses in the auto industry.

author: Tadeu Porto
title: Lula Shows the Power of Workers in the Final Stretch
content:
Lula is entering the final stretch of Brazil’s most contested election, showing the intelligence and energy that define the country’s leading political figure, an asset that is beyond dispute in our history and in the history of the working class.

This moment in the campaign is not just about passion. It reflects the direct result of workers’ ability to steer public debate toward the population’s real needs.

By taking a firm stand and banning online betting, the government showed authority and political courage. It confronted gambling addiction, runaway debt among working families, and money laundering head-on. In doing so, it prioritized protecting family income and family stability, which is what the overwhelming majority of the country’s working class wants.

At the same time, the increase in Bolsa Família payments reaffirms the Lulista hallmark of this project, one that puts the poorest at the center of attention and of the budget, and ensures the state fulfills its essential role of social support.

The impact of these decisions shows up in the most recent polling. According to the BTG/Nexus survey, Lula will win 44% of the vote in the first round, compared with 39% for the second place candidate. In the runoff, the race is a statistical tie, 46% to 44%, leaving no room to be triumphant in victory.
